1:
Everything turns on who the figure is. John Gill runs through the candidates and dismisses them—not the angels at the ascension, not Israel, not Michael returning from a conflict with the king of Persia, since Edom has nothing to do with Persia, and not Judas Maccabaeus, the description being too grand for any mere man; he judges it best to read it of the Messiah, as several Jewish writers ancient and modern do. Adam Clarke spends his note demolishing the reading that makes him Judas Maccabaeus. Could such a man call himself the announcer of righteousness, or speak of the day of vengeance in his heart? His exploits against the Edomites were a battle won with great slaughter, and a successor afterwards forced them to accept circumcision—was it so great an action to force a nation by the sword into Judaism? Clarke adds that the Idumea of the prophet’s day was a different country from the one Judas conquered, and the city Judas took was Hebron, not Bozrah. He concludes the prophecy has no relation to Judas, and holds there is no necessity for supposing it already accomplished. Matthew Henry rejects a different candidate, that the enemies are the Babylonians whom Cyrus conquered: Babylon is always the land of the north, whereas Edom lay south of Jerusalem, so the conqueror would not be returning through it.

The others ask why Edom stands here at all. Charles Ellicott observes that these verses have no apparent connection with what precedes or follows and must be treated as a separate section, though not by a different writer, and then grounds them in history: Edom had been allied against Judah, had carried off Jewish prisoners as slaves, had joined the Assyrian invaders, and later exulted at the capture of Jerusalem. The memory sank deep, so that in later Judaism the rabbis put Edom for Rome when they cursed their oppressors; the prophet takes Edom as representative of all the nearer hereditary enemies. Keil and Delitzsch put the background more strongly: the brother-nation was marked from time immemorial by an implacable hatred that fell on Israel most ruthlessly whenever it was in danger. Henry allows the historical victory but will not stop there: it is named for the old enmity of Esau against Jacob, yet the garments dipped in blood belong in the end to him whose name is called the Word of God. Clarke and John Wesley note that the place-names carry the imagery—Edom signifying red and Bozrah a vintage—so that geography and figure are the same word twice.

The two questions and the answer are read closely. Henry takes the first, who is this, as of a piece with the question Joshua put to the man with the drawn sword; the second he sharpens: is it possible that one with such majesty should be employed in the mean and servile work of treading the winepress? What is really the Redeemer’s glory looks at first like a disparagement—for he took upon him the form of a servant. Ellicott notes that the word rendered travelling describes the gestures of a conqueror exulting, and that the answer is made by the hero-avenger himself, whose claim to righteousness and salvation shows him to be the ideal Servant of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the colour: the seer asks whence the red comes, since it is neither the purple of a king’s robe nor the scarlet of a soldier’s cloak, and the grammar implies it was not the garment’s own colour but something added. Ellicott agrees: the colour is not a soldier’s scarlet dress but blood just shed. Gill draws the contrast devotionally: the garments were white as snow at the transfiguration, whereas this is red, and red not with his own blood but with his enemies’. Wesley hears in the reply both fidelity, that he will perform what he promised, and power to save.
3:
The answer explains the stain, and the emphasis falls on the word alone. John Gill makes the point plainly: what others do by their servants he did by himself, without them. He is careful about which winepress is meant. It is a symbol of the wrath of God, but not of the wrath Christ bore himself as the sinner’s surety, for in that case he was trodden as a vine and not the treader; here it is the wrath he executes on others, wicked men being the clusters cast into it. Adam Clarke reads the clause about the people two ways: it may mean that the conqueror was wholly abandoned by them, but the better meaning is that no man had any part in making the atonement, since no created being could share in a sacrifice of infinite merit. Charles Ellicott takes the figure as the received symbol of the carnage of battle, and says what the hero-conqueror asserts is that the battle was fought single-handed—he had no human allies, though God was with him. He notes that a slight change in the vowel points, adopted by some interpreters, turns the verbs into futures, and prefers the past throughout, since the work of slaughter is clearly thought of as accomplished before the warrior is seen. Keil and Delitzsch render the third clause vividly, that their life-sap spirted upon his clothes so that all his raiment was stained, and note the question whether the word means the trough itself as distinguished from the pressing-house. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense: the enemies of his people are crushed as grapes are crushed, this being a usual metaphor for the utter destruction of a people.

The reason given for the slaughter is a date. Ellicott presses the tenses again: both clauses read better as past, the day of vengeance having been in his heart, since they point to the motive of the action of which the blood-stained garments are the result; and the second phrase he renders the year of my redemption, meaning the work of redeeming his people rather than the people redeemed. Keil and Delitzsch render the same way, a day of vengeance was in my heart and the year of my redemption was come. Gill takes the day as resolved on and fixed with him and desirable to him, so that he has it at heart until the time arrives to avenge the blood of his saints, and applies the vengeance to the destruction of the antichristian powers at the last. Wesley says only that it is to take vengeance on the enemies of his church. Clarke adds two textual observations at this point: the verb rendered I will stain is irregularly formed, compounded of the preterite and future, and a manuscript reads it as a regular past with a pronoun added, which suits the sense better; and one old copy reads that the blood ran down to the earth rather than upon the garments, though the word there is partly effaced.
5:
The isolation of the conqueror is the point everyone fastens on. Charles Ellicott observes that it is emphasised again and again, and that nothing but his own indomitable and righteous zeal against evil had sustained him. John Gill makes the parallel exact: as in the first redemption there were none among the angels or the sons of men to assist him, but the Father only, so in this later salvation the people of God will be reduced to a condition so helpless and forlorn that there will be none to lend a hand, and their deliverance will appear most manifestly to be the sole work of almighty power. John Wesley guards the statement from the wrong inference—not that he needed help, but that he looked to see what men would do, since his people needed it, so that standing or not standing by his people is the same thing as standing or not standing by him; and he notes that the word rendered uphold is a metaphor from a staff that helps one who leans on it. Adam Clarke records a substantial variant here: a good many manuscripts read and my righteousness where the received text has and my fury, a reading he thinks stands on good authority and calls both pleasing and impressive, though the ancient versions favour the common text. At the next verse he notes another, that many copies and two of the versions read and I crushed them instead of and I made them drunken, while the Greek omits the line altogether.

Ellicott takes the last verse in the past throughout—I trod, and so on—and observes that the drinking marks a change of imagery, from the battle to the cup of wrath. He then addresses the use the passage has long been put to. The section has often been applied to the passion, as in the Prayer-Book epistle for the Monday before Easter: in that agony and death it has been said that he was alone and none was with him, and that he trod the winepress of the wrath of God. Ellicott grants that some of the phrases may legitimately be applied so, but denies that this is an interpretation of the passage, which paints a victory and not a passion; the true analogue is the victory of the triumphant Christ in the Revelation. He concedes only this, that from one point of view the agony and the cross were themselves a conflict with the powers of evil, and since he came out of that conflict a conqueror, the words in which the victor over Edom is painted may apply to him there too, in a much remoter analogy. Wesley keeps to the imagery as it stands: they go as it were to and fro, not knowing what to do with themselves, and whatever it is wherein their strength lies is brought down to the very dust.
7:
A new section begins here, and the voices agree on it. Charles Ellicott calls it a psalm of thanksgiving for redemption, and suggests that in the arrangement of the book such a psalm was thought to follow rightly on the dramatic dialogue that had just represented the victory of the Redeemer; it begins with praise and passes to narrative and supplication. John Wesley says the same, that here begins the prophet’s prayer, running to the end of the next chapter. Adam Clarke describes it as a penitential confession of a people in dispersion—cast out of their country, without civil polity or public worship, their temple destroyed and their city desolate, apparently deserted by the God of their fathers. They begin by acknowledging his mercies and the ungrateful returns made on their part, beseech him in consideration of his former loving-kindness, own him as Father and Creator, and deplore their condition; the piece seems designed, Clarke says, as a formulary of humiliation, and the whole is elegiac, pathetic and elegant, though it has suffered much in our copy by the mistakes of transcribers. The prophet, he adds, connects past mercies with the prospect of redemption, making a circle in which eternal goodness revolves.

John Gill reads the opening as the prophet’s own words: having heard what the Lord would do for his people in later times, he calls to mind the favours bestowed of old, and mentions them as pledges of what would be done, to encourage faith in the promise. Matthew Henry treats it as a review made before a prayer, as God’s people in praying were used to look back, and dwells on the plural noun: so plenteous are the springs and so various the streams of divine mercy that the prophet speaks of loving-kindnesses, for if we would count the fruits of it they are more in number than the sand. Henry distinguishes the goodness that is from God, the gifts relating to life and godliness, from the goodness that is in God, since God does good because he is good, and what he bestows is according to his mercies and not our merits. He draws a further rule from the mention of the house of Israel: we must bless God for the mercies enjoyed by others as well as our own, and reckon as bestowed on ourselves what is bestowed on his people.

The second verse is read as the covenant’s starting-point, to which Ellicott says the words throw us back, resting on the assumption that the people would not fail utterly in the fulfilment of their promises. Henry unfolds it: when God brought them out of Egypt and took them into covenant he said, surely they are my people, children that will not lie—that will not dissemble in their covenanting, nor treacherously depart by breaking covenant and starting aside like a broken bow. They had said more than once that all the Lord should say they would do, and thereupon he took them for his peculiar people; God deals faithfully with them, and expects they should deal so with him. Henry presses the description into a definition: God’s people are children that will not lie, for those that will are not his children. Gill takes the possessive strictly: not his people in common with the rest of mankind, but his special people, chosen and taken into covenant, which covenant interest is the ground of every blessing afterwards named; and he extends it to all whom God has chosen, who appear manifestly his by their effectual calling, even where their conduct towards him is not what it should be, as Israel’s was not. Wesley fixes the occasion as the covenant made with the fathers at the coming out of Egypt, glosses the phrase about lying of those who keep the covenant, and identifies the Saviour that follows not with any later deliverer but with Christ himself.
9:
The first clause is famous and textually unsettled. Charles Ellicott lays the alternatives out: read literally it says there was affliction to him, which makes it a statement of divine compassion; but the written Hebrew text gives in all their affliction there was no affliction, meaning that it was as nothing compared with the salvation that came from the Lord, and the received version follows the marginal reading instead. He infers from the strange rendering of both clauses in the Greek—neither a messenger nor an angel, but he himself saved them—that the variation existed at an early date, was a source of perplexity, and drew conjectural emendation to it. John Gill takes the received reading and immediately qualifies it: God is not afflicted properly speaking, since that is not consistent with his nature, being a spirit and impassible, nor with his complete happiness, but the words are said after the manner of men and express his sympathy with his afflicted people, as one friend may feel for another. He adds what follows from it for the sufferer: afflictions come not by chance but according to the will of God, and not in wrath but in love; there is an all of them, and yet not one too many.

On the angel the voices differ in how far they will go. Ellicott renders it the angel of his face, and takes it that God is thought of as working out his purpose of deliverance through the mediation of an angel who is so described either as revealing the highest attributes of God, of which the face is the human symbol, or as standing ever in the immediate presence of the King of kings, ready for any mission; the carrying that follows he calls the same image of fatherly care found elsewhere in the book. John Wesley identifies the angel outright as the one who conducted them through the wilderness and appeared to Moses in the bush, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, and says he carried them in the arms of his power and on the wings of his providence, the phrase about the days of old marking his ancient kindness through many generations.

The turn to rebellion is read as ingratitude and then as something more. Gill lists the occasions—at the Red sea and in the wilderness, by murmuring, unbelief and idolatry, and afterwards in the times of the judges and the prophets—and calls it wretched ingratitude, given how well God had thought of them and how much he had done. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the object of both verbs, which is the Spirit of holiness, and draw a conclusion from it: elsewhere what is resisted and grieved is God himself, or his word, or his providence, whereas here it is the Spirit of holiness, who is thereby distinguished from him as a personal existence. Just as the angel who is his face is marked as a person by his name and by the redeeming activity ascribed to him, so the Spirit of holiness is marked as one by the fact that he can be grieved, and therefore can feel grief; so that in this passage God, the angel of his face and the Spirit of his holiness are distinguished as three. Ellicott makes the same observation independently, that here and in the angel of the Presence we may note a foreshadowing of the trinal personality within the unity of the Godhead which was afterwards to be revealed; and he adds what caused the grief and what followed from it, that it was in the nature of the case the unholiness of the people, and that it involved a change in the manifestation of the divine love, which was now compelled to show itself as wrath. Adam Clarke contributes only a textual note on the conjunction at the head of the last clause.
11:
Who does the remembering is the first question. John Gill takes it of the Lord, who remembered his lovingkindnesses and the covenant made with the fathers and the wonders done at the sea, and therefore determined not to cast the people off but to do as he had done before, putting the questions that follow to stir himself up. Charles Ellicott says the readings vary and the construction is difficult, but the best rendering is probably that his people remembered the ancient days of Moses; in any case it is Israel that remembers, and by that act repents. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way and give the reason: Israel, brought to a right mind in this state of punishment, longed for the better past to return—though they note that the accentuation as it stands would make God the one who remembers. John Wesley canvasses both and adds a third, that the words are the language of the people in exile and should be read as a future, or else that they are God recollecting himself and asking where he is with the former compassion that moved him to help them of old. Adam Clarke notes that some manuscripts read his servant rather than his people, and that one version renders the interrogative as how rather than where, so that the clause becomes a recital instead of a question.

The shepherd is disputed in number. Clarke reports that the copies vary between singular and plural; Ellicott says many give shepherds, probably including Aaron and Miriam among the leaders; Wesley names Moses and Aaron. On the Spirit put within him, Ellicott argues the reference is not to Moses only but to Israel collectively, instancing the gift of the Spirit to the craftsman of the tabernacle, to the seventy elders and to Joshua; Wesley keeps it to the gifts with which God furnished Moses, as proceeding from the Spirit. On the arm that led them, Gill places the agency carefully: the sea was divided by the right hand of Moses and the rod in it, but lest that be attributed to Moses and his rod, the glorious arm of the Lord is named, which held and guided his right hand and whence all the power came. Ellicott renders it the arm of his glory and pictures the unseen Guide accompanying the visible leader, ready to grasp his hand and support him in time of need.

The two images of the passage are read for their ease. Gill observes that they were led through the depths, not the shallows, where the descent was greatest and much filth might have been expected to hinder them. Clarke says they found in the sea bottom no more inconvenience than a horse in the desert, where there is neither stone nor mud, nor a beast in the valley, where all is plain and smooth. Wesley makes it gentler still—with as much ease as a horse led by the bridle, and though the sea was newly divided it was dried and smoothed by the wind God sent, as it were to prepare the way before them—and takes the second figure of a laden beast going warily down the hill, so that they should not be over-travelled or fall through weariness. He notes that the last clause may equally be read as a question closing the enquiry, where is the Spirit that caused them to rest, or else of the rest they were finally led to. Clarke records that the versions differ here, reading conducted them or conducted him where the received text has caused him to rest. Keil and Delitzsch mark the structural turn: with this verse the description passes into direct address, and by that change, with the thought that Israel is now in a condition that makes it look back longingly to the old redemption, the way is prepared for the petitions that follow.
15:
The prayer proper begins here. Matthew Henry says the foregoing praises were its introduction, and calls it affectionate, importunate and pleading, calculated for the time of the captivity: as the people had promises prepared for that time of need, so they had prayers, that they might take with them words in turning to the Lord, the words being of God’s own inditing; and some interpreters, he notes, take the prayer to look further still. John Gill marks the same division, the prayer of the church running from here to the end of the next chapter. On the request Henry is precise: they knew God sees all, but prayed that he would regard them, looking on them with the compassion with which he looked on the affliction of his people in Egypt; and in begging that he would only look down and behold, they in effect appealed to his justice against their enemies while leaving the manner of relief to his wisdom. Gill draws the same distinction, that what is asked is not the general view God always takes but a special look of love and grace. John Wesley says the prophet begins here to expostulate with God, arguing from the goodness of his nature and the greatness of his works, and that behold means not barely to see but to see with regard.

The address to heaven is read two ways. Henry takes the phrase devotionally: God’s holiness is his glory, and it is an encouragement to praying people who desire to be holy as he is holy that he dwells in a holy place. Charles Ellicott hears something sharper, a latent remonstrance, as though the Lord, like an Eastern king, had withdrawn into the recesses of his palace and ceased to show the care he had shown of old; and on the phrase about the sounding of the bowels he observes that the words jar upon modern ears but were to the Hebrew what the sighs of thy heart would be to us. Wesley puts the question plainest—what is become of that love which of old would not let thee suffer thy people to be wronged? Henry adds the petition that follows, that God would return and change his way towards them, since his people dread nothing more than his departures and desire nothing more than his returns. Adam Clarke notes only that the copies vary between singular and plural in the word for strength, and between from me and from us at the close.

The appeal to fatherhood is the strongest thing here. Gill says the church pleads her relation to God in a strong manner, faith of interest continuing though he hid his face, and insists the relation stands neither on creation, by which he is father to all men, nor on national adoption, but on special adopting grace. Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as justifying the whole prayer: the Lord is Israel’s Father, his creative might and the counsels of his love having called the nation into being—though the word has not yet, they add, the unrestricted sense of the New Testament Our Father. The patriarchs, they note, could not help, having been taken from this world and being unable to interfere in the history of their people. Ellicott renders it for Abraham is ignorant of us and finds the passage striking as anticipating the New Testament thought that the fatherhood of God rests on something other than hereditary descent and extends to all mankind: Abraham might disclaim his degenerate descendants, and the Lord would still recognise them. Wesley reads it of one who was their father after the flesh but is dead and so ignorant of their condition, and observes that the plea gains force because their Father was also their Redeemer. Clarke reports a manuscript reading that turns the last clause into a petition: for the sake of thy name deliver us.
17:
The hardest question here is who caused the wandering. John Gill is emphatic that these are not the words of wicked men charging their errors upon God as though he were their author, but of the truly godly, confessing their own wandering and the hardness of their hearts, and wondering that their tender Father should suffer them to err—by withholding his grace, withdrawing his presence, and chastising them so sorely that they lay under temptation to desert his worship. Adam Clarke resolves it as a Hebraism for why hast thou permitted us to err, of the same kind as the petition not to be led into temptation; John Wesley glosses both clauses so, suffered us to err and suffered it to be hardened. Keil and Delitzsch do not soften it. When men have obstinately rejected the grace of God, he withdraws it judicially, gives them up to their wanderings and makes their heart incapable of faith; the history of Israel from the prophet’s own commission onwards has been such a judgment of hardening, a curse eating deeper and spreading wider. Yet they add the qualification the prayer depends on: the great mass are lost, but not without possibility of deliverance for the better part, which now appeals to the mercy of God. Charles Ellicott states the fear plainly—have their sins led God to abandon them and harden their hearts as he hardened Pharaoh’s?—and names the refuge: against that thought the prophet finds shelter where alone men can, in prayer, and in pleading the promise and the election of grace, to which God remains faithful though men are faithless. Conscious that they have no power to return to him, they can ask him to return to them. Wesley notes the plea is made for the sake of the little remnant that are his servants.

The next verse is textually vexed. Gill offers three ways of taking it: of the land, possessed some fourteen hundred years, a little while compared with the for ever promised; of their enjoying it in peace only briefly; or of the sanctuary, which stood little more than four centuries. Ellicott renders it that for a little while have they possessed thy sanctuary, or, with a variant, thy holy mountain, and grounds the plea on the promise that the inheritance was to be everlasting, so that measured against it the possession was short—the failure aggravated by the enemies treading down the sanctuary. Clarke finds the received rendering defective, its verb needing an object supplied. He suspects a mistake in the text and prefers the Greek, which read mountain where ours has people, so that the sense becomes: not only have our enemies taken the holy mountain and trodden down the sanctuary, but worse has befallen us, for thou hast long since utterly cast us off. Keil and Delitzsch report the attempt to make the adversaries the subject of the verb, and show that the phrase for a little time will not bear it.

The last verse divides the voices completely. Gill and Wesley take it as an assertion of covenant standing: we are thine, thy children and thy people, some reading we are thine of old; whereas the nations named next never were in covenant, never owned God nor were owned by him—which is the argument the petitioners use. Ellicott denies the construction. The word thine, as the italics show, is not in the Hebrew, and its insertion distorts the meaning; the sense is that we are become as those over whom thou hast never ruled, upon whom thy name has never been called. What the prophet presents as a plea is then not the contrast between Israel and the heathen, but the fact that Israel has been left to sink to the level of the heathen who had not known God—and he asks whether that thought would not move the Lord to remember his covenant.
